A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Intelligent Go-Explore, with matching core algorithms and experiments. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added, and removed material to be identified.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, archive-size measurements, and GPT-4/GPT-3.5 experiments in Sections 4–5.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds visual BabyAI evaluation, a Classic Go-Explore comparison, additional foundation models, and prompt-robustness results.

M1.justification: The three FM-guided stages, state-conditional action history, and two archive-filtering options remain unchanged. Visual observations and alternative foundation models instantiate the existing framework. Algorithm 1's explicit set unions clarify the accumulation already described in v1 rather than establish a different procedure.

E1.justification: v3 retains Game of 24, BabyAI-Text, and TextWorld, and adds BabyAI-Visual across all five task families (Section 4.2, Figure 3b). Partially observable images replace textual observations, substantially extending evaluated input conditions. Stochastic environments and real-world applications remain discussion rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds Classic Go-Explore (Visitation Frequency) on Game of 24, BabyAI PutNextTo, and TextWorld Cooking Game. This heuristic comparator differs from v1's uniform-random component ablations. Comparator membership in the retained benchmark experiments otherwise remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled prompt-removal experiments across three tasks and evaluates IGE and agent baselines using GPT-4, Llama-3 400B, and Claude Sonnet 3.5 on Game of 24. This replaces v1's GPT-4/GPT-3.5 sensitivity setting across three tasks. The original task budgets and GPT-4 sampling settings remain, but the added controls and model configurations substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a substantive robustness study testing dependence on few-shot examples and task-specific hints against agent baselines. Model-dependence analysis is also reworked. Existing component ablations and the Cooking Game trajectory remain; archive-size analysis moves from v1 Table 3 to v3 Appendix C.1/Table 4 with unchanged measurements.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 100 Game of 24 evaluation problems/seeds, 25 seeds for the other principal tasks, 95% bootstrap intervals with 10,000 resamples, and chi-square significance testing. New tables invoke the existing evaluation and uncertainty conventions. Inconsistent interval values do not establish a changed estimator or run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds visual BabyAI success rates of 96%, 60%, 60%, 8%, and 52%; Game of 24 IGE results of 98% with Llama-3 400B and 86% with Claude Sonnet 3.5; and prompt-variant results of 96%, 68%, and 72% across the three representative tasks. Classic Go-Explore results are added, while GPT-3.5 results of 57%, 0%, and 0% disappear. Original benchmark curves and ablations remain. New reporting is not fully reconciled: Table 3 gives the GPT-4 naive baseline 70%, whereas retained Figure 2 stays below 50%, and repeated confidence intervals differ between tables.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, simulator-return assumption, language-model probability expression, and Game of 24 search-space bound remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs that are substantively added or revised in v3.

C1.justification: The central contribution—replacing Go-Explore's handcrafted choices with foundation-model judgments—remains intact. v3 explicitly presents demonstrated visual capability and consistent improvements across multiple model families as contributions. Multimodal applicability was already proposed in v1, but its demonstrated scope was limited to text.

C2.justification: v3 shifts the model-choice interpretation from GPT-4 outperforming GPT-3.5 toward benefits across model families, and interprets the new prompt experiments as evidence of robustness. Appendices D.4 and F substantially expand explanations of environmental grounding, hallucinations, stochastic applicability, model bias, and scalability alternatives. These are substantive interpretations and qualifications beyond v1's shorter discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the visual-environment prompt and specifies prompt deletions used in robustness experiments. It also clarifies archive/history updates and discusses existing invalid-output handling in dedicated appendix subsections. Original GPT-4 versions, sampling parameters, budgets, cost figures, and code-access information remain; the GPT-3.5 implementation reference persists despite removal of its results.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through discussions of GFlowNets, hierarchical search/MCTS, Minecraft agents, and robotic foundation models. The Tree of Thoughts comparison now emphasizes environment-grounded states versus generated thoughts and flexible search strategies. The existing FM-as-judge discussion is relocated to Appendix F, rather than removed.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative remains recognizable. Selected passages in the abstract, introduction, archive explanation, model analysis, related work, and conclusion are rewritten. Background headings are reformatted, citations become author–year, and appendix organization expands with relocated analysis and related work; this is a limited restructuring of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 3 becomes a two-panel text/visual comparison, and Table 1 adds an image observation. Table 2 expands into a full-width display, the original two-part Table 3 is reorganized, archive-size results move to an appendix table, and new model-comparison and prompt-robustness tables appear. Typography, headings, and page headers also change throughout.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's text-only evidence, visual evaluation and the new baseline, model, and prompt comparisons provide useful tests of generality and dependence on heuristics. However, unreconciled Game of 24 scores between Figure 2 and Table 3, inconsistent repeated confidence intervals, and robustness prose understating the Cooking Game's 20-point drop weaken the additions. The broader evidence and clearer explanations yield a limited net improvement, with reporting problems constraining confidence in stronger claims.
